{{Short description|Type of statistical estimator}}
In [[statistics]], '''Hodges' estimator'''<ref>{{harvtxt|Vaart|1998|p=109}}</ref> (or the '''Hodges–Le Cam estimator'''<ref>{{harvtxt|Kale|1985}}</ref>), named for [[Joseph Lawson Hodges Jr.|Joseph Hodges]], is a famous [[counterexample]] demonstrating the existence of an [[estimator]] which is "[[superefficient]]",<ref>{{harvtxt|Bickel|1998|p=21}}</ref> i.e. it attains smaller asymptotic variance than regular [[efficient estimator]]s. The existence of such a counterexample is the reason for the introduction of the notion of [[regular estimator]]s.

Hodges' estimator improves upon a regular estimator at a single point. In general, any superefficient estimator may surpass a regular estimator at most on a set of [[Lebesgue measure]] zero.<ref>{{harvtxt|Vaart|1998|p=116}}</ref>

Although Hodges discovered the estimator he never published it; the first publication was in the doctoral thesis of [[Lucien Le Cam]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Le Cam |first=Lucien M. |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/005761137 |title=On some asymptotic properties of maximum likelihood estimates and related Bayes' estimates. |last2=University of California |first2=Berkeley. |date=1953 |publisher=University of California press |series=University of California publications in statistics; v. 1, no. 11 |location=Berkeley}}</ref>

== Construction ==
Suppose <math>\hat{\theta}_n</math> is a "common" estimator for some parameter <math>\theta</math>: it is [[consistent estimator|consistent]], and converges to some [[asymptotic distribution]] <math>L_\theta</math> (usually this is a [[normal distribution]] with mean zero and variance which may depend on <math>\theta</math>) at the <math>\sqrt{n}</math>-rate:
: <math>
    \sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \theta)\ \xrightarrow{d}\ L_\theta\ .
  </math>

Then the '''Hodges' estimator''' <math>\hat{\theta}_n^H</math> is defined as<ref>{{harvtxt|Stoica|Ottersten|1996|p=135}}</ref>
: <math>
    \hat\theta_n^H = \begin{cases}\hat\theta_n, & \text{if } |\hat\theta_n| \geq n^{-1/4}, \text{ and} \\ 0, & \text{if } |\hat\theta_n| < n^{-1/4}.\end{cases}
  </math>
This estimator is equal to <math>\hat{\theta}_n</math> everywhere except on the small interval <math>[-n^{-1/4},n^{-1/4}]</math>, where it is equal to zero. It is not difficult to see that this estimator is [[consistent estimator|consistent]] for <math>\theta</math>, and its [[asymptotic distribution]] is<ref>{{harvtxt|Vaart|1998|p=109}}</ref>
: <math>\begin{align}
    & n^\alpha(\hat\theta_n^H - \theta) \ \xrightarrow{d}\ 0, \qquad\text{when } \theta = 0, \\
    &\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n^H - \theta)\ \xrightarrow{d}\ L_\theta, \quad \text{when } \theta\neq 0,
  \end{align}</math>
for any <math>\alpha\in\mathbb{R}</math>. Thus this estimator has the same asymptotic distribution as <math>\hat{\theta}_n</math> for all <math>\theta\neq 0</math>, whereas for <math>\theta=0</math> the [[rate of convergence]] becomes arbitrarily fast. This estimator is ''superefficient'', as it surpasses the asymptotic behavior of the efficient estimator <math>\hat{\theta}_n</math> at least at one point <math>\theta=0</math>.

It is not true that the Hodges estimator is equivalent to the [[sample mean]],  but much better when the true mean is 0. The correct interpretation is that, for finite <math>n</math>, the  truncation can lead to worse square error than the sample mean  estimator for <math>E[X]</math> close to 0, as is shown in the example in the following section.<ref>Vaart AW van der. ''Asymptotic Statistics''. Cambridge University Press; 1998.</ref>

Le Cam shows that this behaviour is typical: superefficiency at the point θ implies the existence of a sequence <math>\theta_n \rightarrow \theta</math> such that <math>\liminf_{n\to\infty} E \theta_n \ell (\sqrt n (\hat \theta_n - \theta_n ))</math> is strictly larger than the [[Cramér–Rao bound]]. For the extreme case where the asymptotic risk at θ is zero, the <math>\liminf_{n\to\infty}</math> is even infinite for a sequence <math>\theta_n \rightarrow \theta</math>.<ref>van der Vaart, A. W., & Wellner, J. A. (1996). Weak Convergence and Empirical Processes. In Springer Series in Statistics. Springer New York. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-2545-2</ref>

In general, superefficiency may only be attained on a subset of Lebesgue measure zero of the parameter space <math>\Theta</math>.<ref>Vaart AW van der. ''Asymptotic Statistics''. Cambridge University Press; 1998.</ref>

== Example ==
[[Image:Hodges estimator risk function.svg|right|thumb|The [[mean square error]] (times ''n'') of Hodges' estimator. Blue curve corresponds to {{nowrap|''n'' {{=}} 5}}, purple to {{nowrap|''n'' {{=}} 50}}, and olive to {{nowrap|''n'' {{=}} 500}}.<ref>{{harvtxt|Vaart|1998|p=110}}</ref>]]

Suppose ''x''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''x<sub>n</sub>'' is an [[independent and identically distributed]] (IID) random sample from normal distribution {{nowrap|''N''(''θ'', 1)}} with unknown mean but known variance. Then the common estimator for the population mean ''θ'' is the [[arithmetic mean]] of all observations: <math>\bar{x}</math>. The corresponding Hodges' estimator will be <math>\hat\theta^H_n \;=\; \bar{x}\cdot\mathbf{1}\{|\bar x|\,\geq\,n^{-1/4}\}</math>, where '''1'''{...} denotes the [[indicator function]].

The [[mean square error]] (scaled by ''n'') associated with the regular estimator <span style="text-decoration:overline">''x''</span> is constant and equal to 1 for all ''θ''{{'}}s. At the same time the mean square error of the Hodges' estimator <math>\hat\theta_n^H</math> behaves erratically in the vicinity of zero, and even becomes unbounded as {{nowrap|''n'' → ∞}}. This demonstrates that the Hodges' estimator is not [[regular estimator|regular]], and its asymptotic properties are not adequately described by limits of the form (''θ'' fixed, {{nowrap|''n'' → ∞}}).
